why: The job is stateful, runs longer than an hour, and cannot be interrupted. A container run as an ECS task on Fargate has no maximum runtime and runs on on-demand capacity, and EventBridge Scheduler can start it on a weekly cron schedule without any servers to manage.

others.B: Lambda functions time out after 15 minutes, so a job of an hour or more cannot run in one.
others.C: Spot Instances can be reclaimed at two minutes' notice, which breaks a stateful job that cannot be interrupted.
others.D: DataSync moves data between storage systems and cannot run analysis code.

tip: If a job runs longer than 15 minutes, rule out Lambda. If it cannot be interrupted, rule out Spot.

why: Amazon Security Lake automatically collects security data from AWS services and third-party sources, normalizes it to the OCSF format, and stores it in an S3 data lake that it manages, across accounts and Regions. That gives central security analysis with the least development effort.

others.A: Lake Formation with Glue crawlers means building and maintaining your own ingestion pipelines and schema normalization for security logs.
others.B: A custom Lambda collector that writes CSV files is development-heavy and does not normalize the data or cover many sources.
others.D: DMS migrates databases. It does not collect security logs, and RDS is not a security data lake.

tip: When a question says to centralize security data in OCSF across the organization, the answer is Security Lake.

why: A transit gateway is a regional hub-and-spoke router. Each VPC attaches once, and route tables control which VPCs can talk to each other and to the shared services VPC. This scales to more than 100 application VPCs without a full mesh of connections, so it has the least administrative overhead.

others.A: Software VPN tunnels between VPCs mean managing many appliances and tunnels, which does not scale.
others.B: VPC peering is not transitive, so the applications would need a full mesh of n(n-1)/2 peering connections to reach each other.
others.C: Direct Connect links on-premises networks to AWS. It does not connect one VPC to another.

tip: When many VPCs must reach each other or a shared VPC, choose Transit Gateway.

why: ECS Anywhere uses the EXTERNAL launch type to register on-premises servers with the same ECS control plane, and Fargate runs the cloud containers. Together they give one container platform across on-premises and cloud. An Application Load Balancer is the layer 7 load balancer meant for HTTP traffic to the cloud ECS services.

others.C: A Network Load Balancer works at layer 4. For HTTP traffic, an ALB is the better choice.
others.D: Fargate runs only in AWS and cannot run containers on premises.
others.E: ECS Anywhere cannot use the Fargate launch type. On-premises capacity must use the EXTERNAL launch type.

tip: ECS Anywhere uses the EXTERNAL launch type. Fargate is never available on premises.

why: RDS for SQL Server is managed: AWS handles patching, backups, and failover, which cuts operational overhead. Multi-AZ adds high availability for critical data, and KMS encryption at rest improves security. The engine stays SQL Server, so the relational workload does not need to be redesigned.

others.A: SQL Server on EC2 leaves patching, backups, and high availability with the company, so overhead does not drop.
others.C: S3 with Macie is object storage and data discovery. It cannot replace a relational SQL Server database.
others.D: DynamoDB is NoSQL and would require a rewrite, and CloudWatch Logs does not secure data.

why: An Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones replaces unhealthy instances and scales with demand. An ALB spreads traffic across the zones. AWS WAF can be associated with an ALB, which makes this the highly available design with WAF in the right place.

others.B: A cluster placement group puts instances in a single AZ, which lowers availability, and WAF cannot be attached to a placement group.
others.C: Two fixed instances with no Auto Scaling cannot self-heal or scale, so availability is lower.
others.D: WAF cannot be attached to an Auto Scaling group. It attaches to ALB, CloudFront, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito, App Runner, or Verified Access.

tip: WAF attaches to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, AppSync, Cognito user pools, App Runner, and Verified Access. It never attaches to EC2 instances or Auto Scaling groups.

why: S3 access points give each application its own endpoint with its own policy, and that policy can be scoped to the application's prefix and specific actions. This gives granular access per prefix on one bucket without copying data or writing one large bucket policy, so it has the least operational overhead.

others.B: Setting per-object ACLs with Batch Operations is hard to manage, and AWS recommends disabling ACLs.
others.C: Replicating data into separate buckets per application duplicates storage and adds replication to manage.
others.D: Replication duplicates the data needlessly, because access points work directly on the existing bucket.

tip: Many applications sharing one bucket, each limited to its own prefix, points to S3 Access Points.

why: Each image needs only 2 minutes and 512 MB, which fits well within Lambda's 15-minute and 10 GB limits. S3 event notifications send messages to SQS, which buffers bursts, and Lambda polls the queue and is billed only while it processes. Nothing sits idle, so this is the most cost-effective option.

others.B: A Reserved Instance runs and is billed around the clock even when there are no uploads.
others.C: An ECS container instance is an always-on EC2 host, so you pay for idle capacity.
others.D: Elastic Beanstalk runs always-on EC2 instances and adds more infrastructure than the task needs.

tip: Short, event-driven, low-memory work is a Lambda job.

why: Global Accelerator supports both TCP and UDP. It gives static anycast IPs, sends users over the AWS global network to the nearest healthy endpoint, and fails over quickly. Network Load Balancers also handle TCP and UDP: one in each Region fronts the EC2 instances, and another reaches the on-premises UDP servers as IP targets.

others.B: CloudFront serves HTTP and HTTPS content. It does not accelerate arbitrary TCP or UDP workloads.
others.C: Application Load Balancers handle only HTTP and HTTPS, so they cannot carry raw TCP or UDP traffic.
others.E: An ALB cannot carry the UDP traffic to the on-premises workload.

tip: For UDP or non-HTTP TCP, choose NLB plus Global Accelerator, not ALB plus CloudFront.

why: Recycle Bin retention rules keep deleted EBS snapshots for a set period, here 7 days, and they can be restored during that window. Accidental deletions can be undone, snapshots expire from the bin automatically so nothing is kept forever, and no code changes are needed.

others.A: Denying deletion through IAM would stop the cleanup script from removing expired snapshots, so snapshots would pile up indefinitely.
others.B: Copying snapshots to another Region costs more, and the same script could still delete the copies.
others.D: You cannot copy EBS snapshots straight into a chosen S3 storage class. It would also take custom work and still not guard against deletion.

tip: For accidental deletion of EBS snapshots or AMIs, use Recycle Bin.

why: A presigned URL grants temporary access to one specific object using the creator's credentials. The bucket stays private, and access is granted per request and expires on its own, which follows least-privilege best practice.

others.A: A gateway VPC endpoint is a network path from a VPC. It does not authorize CloudFormation to read the template, and CloudFormation does not run inside your VPC.
others.B: An API Gateway proxy to S3 adds complexity and more attack surface for no benefit.
others.D: Making the object public, even for a short time, breaks the block-public-access requirement and best practice.

tip: For temporary, scoped access to a single private S3 object, use a presigned URL.

why: IAM Identity Center gives the external engineers federated console access to every account in the organization through permission sets, without long-lived IAM users. Session Manager gives them audited operating system shells on private instances through the SSM Agent and an instance profile, with no SSH keys, open inbound ports, or bastion host.

others.B: Local IAM users in each account mean long-lived credentials, and Session Manager does not hand out console credentials.
others.C: Opening SSH and handing out key pairs and IAM user credentials increases exposure and key-management risk.
others.D: A bastion host with SSH keys and local IAM users is less secure and has more overhead than Session Manager with Identity Center.

tip: For secure shell access to private instances, choose Session Manager. For workforce console access across an organization, choose IAM Identity Center.

why: An RDS for PostgreSQL read replica in the same Region takes the reporting reads off the primary using asynchronous replication. Keeping it in us-east-1 avoids cross-Region data transfer charges and extra latency, which makes it the cheapest way to restore performance.

others.A: A cross-Region replica adds inter-Region transfer cost and replication lag with no benefit for this requirement.
others.B: In a Multi-AZ DB instance deployment, the standby cannot serve reads. It exists only for failover.
others.C: A separate database fed by DMS logical replication costs more and needs more management than a native read replica.

tip: A classic Multi-AZ standby is not readable. Multi-AZ DB clusters have readable standbys, but read replicas are the usual answer for offloading reads.

why: By default, EC2 sends CloudWatch metrics every 5 minutes. Detailed monitoring sends them every 1 minute, which meets the requirement of no more than 2 minutes, and the metrics can be analyzed in CloudWatch straight away with no pipelines to build.

others.A: Exporting logs to Redshift and QuickSight is heavy and does not change the 5-minute metric interval.
others.C: Fetching logs with a Lambda function does not improve EC2 metric granularity and adds custom work.
others.D: An S3, Redshift, and QuickSight log pipeline is complex and is not near-real-time performance monitoring.

tip: Basic monitoring is 5 minutes, detailed monitoring is 1 minute, and high-resolution custom metrics go down to 1 second.

why: About 150 uploads a day is a low, event-driven volume. An S3 event notification that invokes Lambda creates each thumbnail on upload, and you pay only for those short invocations, with no idle compute, so it is the most cost-effective option.

others.A: A long-running EMR cluster is far too costly for creating a few thumbnails.
others.B: An always-on memory-optimized EC2 instance is billed constantly for very little work.
others.D: S3 Storage Lens provides storage analytics and cannot invoke Lambda on uploads.

why: S3 Inventory gives a list of all objects, which can be filtered to exclude the data that must be kept. S3 Batch Operations then runs a Lambda function on each object in the manifest to delete it, at the scale of millions of objects, and the whole process is serverless.

others.A: Running a CLI script on an EC2 instance is not serverless.
others.B: AWS Batch runs compute jobs on EC2 or Fargate and has no native logic for deleting selected S3 objects. It also needs more setup.
others.C: Glue crawlers catalog data schemas. They do not list objects by age, and the deletion script still needs somewhere to run.

tip: For large-scale actions on S3 objects, use S3 Inventory as the manifest and Batch Operations to run the action.

why: Giving each Lambda function its own execution role, with only the S3 permissions that function needs, follows least privilege. Only functions whose roles allow access can read the bucket, and each grant can be scoped and audited on its own.

others.A: A shared role with full bucket access gives every function more than it needs, which breaks least privilege.
others.B: Lambda functions in a VPC have no fixed IP addresses, and VPC endpoint policies use endpoint IDs, not IPs, so IP-based control is unreliable.
others.D: Bucket policies identify callers by principal, here the execution role. A function ARN is not a principal that the policy can match on.

why: S3 with CloudFront serves the static frontend globally and securely, using OAC and edge caching. Lambda behind API Gateway removes servers from the microservices, and RDS for MySQL is a managed database. Every layer is managed, so this has the least operational overhead.

others.A: Leaving MySQL on an EC2 Reserved Instance means the company still manages the database.
others.C: A Network Load Balancer cannot have Lambda functions as targets. Only an ALB supports Lambda targets.
others.D: Without CloudFront the frontend is not delivered globally, and MySQL stays self-managed on EC2.

why: ElastiCache for Redis gives sub-millisecond reads and its sorted sets suit leaderboards and rankings. Redis also persists data to disk with RDB snapshots and AOF and supports replication, so the data survives a restart, and it is a managed service.

others.A: S3 behind CloudFront is not built for near-real-time updates to rankings.
others.B: Self-managed EC2 instances in several Regions add heavy operational overhead and no built-in ranking features.
others.D: Memcached has no persistence or replication, so the data is lost on restart.

tip: Leaderboards and rankings point to Redis sorted sets. If the cache must persist, rule out Memcached.

why: A separate customer managed KMS key for each customer isolates each customer's encryption. Key policies and grants give fine-grained access control, and CloudTrail logs every key use. KMS is centralized and managed, so the overhead stays low.

others.A: Storing raw keys in an S3 bucket is insecure and is not centralized key management.
others.B: Running your own hardware security appliance adds a lot of operational overhead compared with native KMS keys.
others.C: A single key for all customers does not encrypt each customer's data separately.

why: An ALB spreads web traffic across an Auto Scaling group that scales with demand. An SQS queue holds orders that have not been processed yet, so none are lost during spikes, and RDS Multi-AZ stores the processed orders durably with failover. The tiers are decoupled and resilient.

others.A: A NAT gateway carries outbound traffic from private subnets. It does not load balance incoming web traffic.
others.B: Redshift is a data warehouse, not an order store, and the NLB-to-ALB chain adds nothing.
others.C: A Gateway Load Balancer is for third-party network appliances and cannot store orders.

why: Millions of 10 KB files cost a lot as separate S3 objects: each object incurs request charges, and Glacier Instant Retrieval bills each object as at least 128 KB. Bundling them into large archives removes most of that. Glacier Instant Retrieval gives immediate access at low storage cost for data read once or twice a year, and a lifecycle rule then moves the archives to Deep Archive, the cheapest class, for the 7-year retention.

others.B: Standard-IA costs more than Glacier Instant Retrieval for data read so rarely, and Instant Retrieval is a poor long-term archive tier compared with Deep Archive.
others.C: Unbundled 10 KB objects are billed at the 128 KB minimum in Glacier Instant Retrieval, and each also carries per-object transition charges, while Flexible Retrieval costs more than Deep Archive.
others.D: Unbundled small objects incur Standard-IA's 128 KB minimum charge and per-object transition costs, and Standard-IA storage costs more than Glacier Instant Retrieval.

tip: Very small objects cost more in IA and Glacier classes because of the minimum billable object size and per-request fees. Combine them first.

why: An io1 volume tops out at 64,000 IOPS, and this volume is already at that limit. Attaching several io1 volumes and striping them with LVM in RAID 0 adds their IOPS and throughput together. That is the only listed way to get more performance.

others.B: io1 cannot be provisioned above 64,000 IOPS per volume. Going higher needs io2 Block Express.
others.C: Making the volume bigger does not raise IOPS past the 64,000 ceiling.
others.D: A storage optimized instance adds local instance store, not EBS performance, and a memory optimized instance suits Oracle better.

tip: When a single volume is at its maximum IOPS, stripe several volumes with RAID 0 or switch to io2 Block Express.

why: SNS gives managed pub/sub that fans events out to many subscribers. API Gateway HTTP APIs cost about 70% less than REST APIs and have lower latency. That makes HTTP API, then Lambda, then SNS the most cost-effective serverless event-driven design.

others.A: SQS is a point-to-point queue, not pub/sub. Each message goes to one consumer.
others.B: This design works but uses the more expensive REST API without needing its extra features.
others.C: Kinesis with enhanced fan-out costs far more for shards and per-consumer throughput and is meant for streaming.

tip: If no REST-only feature such as API keys, usage plans, or WAF is needed, an HTTP API is the cheaper choice.

why: The tightly coupled application can run on only one instance, so the fix is to scale vertically to an instance type with more CPU. An Auto Scaling group with min and max of 1 still replaces a failed instance. An RDS read replica takes read requests off the primary, which improves read performance.

others.B: Read replicas are read-only, so sending write traffic to the replica would fail.
others.C: A maximum of 2 would run a second instance, which the application cannot support, and it does not offload reads.
others.D: Making the RDS instance bigger helps but costs more than a read replica, which is the standard way to offload read traffic.

why: IAM roles with fine-grained, least-privilege policies give developers temporary credentials limited to what each one needs. That prevents unauthorized access to sensitive data and avoids long-lived shared secrets.

others.A: Sharing credentials removes accountability and is a serious security anti-pattern.
others.C: Long-lived access keys are risky, and creating them does nothing to scope permissions.
others.D: Cognito user pools authenticate users of your application, not developers who need access to AWS resources.

why: Compute Optimizer studies CloudWatch usage and recommends the right instance size, so each instance is not starved of CPU. An Auto Scaling group behind an ALB then scales out horizontally and spreads instances across AZs, which improves availability. Together they fix the CPU problem cost-effectively.

others.B: An AMI and launch template are setup steps for an Auto Scaling group. By themselves they neither fix the CPU problem nor add availability.
others.C: Auto Scaling groups and ALBs scale horizontally by adding instances, not vertically.
others.D: Compute Optimizer recommends instance types and sizes, which is vertical rightsizing. It does not plan horizontal scaling.

why: IAM Access Analyzer reports unused access, such as unused roles, users, access keys, passwords, and permissions, and it generates policies from recorded activity. It can use the organization as its zone of trust, so it finds over-permissioned IAM users across all accounts with little effort.

others.A: Network Access Analyzer examines network reachability paths, not IAM permissions.
others.B: A CloudWatch alarm on resource changes does not judge whether a user has excess permissions.
others.D: Amazon Inspector scans EC2, ECR, and Lambda for software vulnerabilities, not IAM policies.

tip: For over-privileged IAM users or unused access, use IAM Access Analyzer.

why: S3 Object Lock in compliance mode means no user, including the root user, can overwrite or delete a protected object version, or shorten its retention, until the retention period ends. That is the fixed-period protection that regulations require.

others.A: In governance mode, users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention can still delete or change objects, so it is not strict enough for regulatory compliance.
others.C: Versioning with an expiration rule deletes data and does not stop anyone from deleting or modifying it.
others.D: Moving objects to Glacier changes the storage class but does not protect them from deletion.

tip: Compliance mode means nobody can delete, even root. Governance mode lets privileged users bypass the lock.

why: Compute Optimizer gives rightsizing recommendations for the CPU and memory of ECS services on Fargate, based on CloudWatch usage. Rightsizing a resource-intensive task cuts cost while keeping regular Fargate capacity, which a customer-facing app that runs 24/7 needs to stay highly available.

others.A: Running third-party load tests and analyzing them by hand takes more effort and is less reliable than Compute Optimizer's automated recommendations.
others.B: Fargate Spot tasks can be interrupted at two minutes' notice, which is risky for customer-facing bursts on a workload that must be highly available.
others.C: Running steady-state traffic on Fargate Spot would put the always-on customer workload at risk of interruption.

why: Shield Advanced gives managed DDoS detection and mitigation for ALB and Route 53 hosted zones. It includes the Shield Response Team, and with proactive engagement the SRT contacts you when a protected resource's health checks show an attack. That proactive engagement is the deciding requirement.

others.A: AWS Config checks resource configuration compliance and does not detect DDoS attacks.
others.B: WAF rate-based rules help against layer 7 floods, but WAF alone has no managed response team or proactive engagement.
others.C: GuardDuty does not analyze ALB access logs or take automated DDoS-prevention actions.

tip: The words proactive engagement or DDoS response team mean Shield Advanced.

why: The keyed answer reasons that AWS Shield Advanced protects the NLB from attack traffic with managed DDoS detection and mitigation, without changing the existing architecture.

others.A: AWS WAF cannot be associated with a Network Load Balancer. It works only with layer 7 resources.
others.B: The key treats rebuilding the NLB with a security group as more of an architectural change. This is disputed (see flag).
others.C: A second NLB in parallel adds complexity and does not secure the existing endpoint.

tip: An NLB can have security groups only if they are attached when it is created. You cannot add them to an NLB created without them.
flag: Shield Advanced protects against DDoS attacks, not unauthorized access. NLBs now support security groups, but only when they are created, so recreating the NLB with a security group that allows only trusted IP addresses (B) is the better answer.

why: Publishing to an SNS topic encrypted with a customer managed key needs three permissions. The topic's resource policy must allow the Lambda function's role to call sns:Publish. The KMS key policy must allow kms:GenerateDataKey and kms:Decrypt. The Lambda execution role must have IAM permissions for sns:Publish and for that KMS key.

others.B: Customer managed keys already are SSE-KMS keys, and switching to the AWS managed key would weaken control over PHI encryption.
others.D: Lambda calls SNS using its execution role, so the topic policy names the role ARN as the principal, not the function ARN.
others.E: API Gateway is not needed for Lambda to publish to SNS and adds nothing to authorization.

why: Keeping the web portal on On-Demand EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group avoids any code changes and gives uninterrupted capacity for 100% uptime. The extraction program runs only occasionally, so running it as a Lambda function triggered on upload costs nothing while idle and scales automatically. That is the least implementation effort.

others.B: Spot Instances can be interrupted, which conflicts with 100% uptime, and launching instances for each upload is slow and complex.
others.C: A Savings Plan commits spend to always-on capacity for a program that runs only now and then, and it changes nothing about the architecture.
others.D: Rebuilding the portal on S3 and Lambda requires code changes, which the company does not want.

why: For SNS to invoke a Lambda function in another account, two policies are needed. The function's resource-based policy, added with lambda add-permission, must allow sns.amazonaws.com from the production topic's ARN to invoke it. The topic's access policy must allow the administrator account to subscribe the function to the topic. Both together complete the cross-account subscription.

others.B: An SQS buffer is not required, because SNS can invoke a Lambda function in another account directly.
others.D: EventBridge does not capture SNS notifications as events in this way, so this adds an unnecessary hop.
others.E: S3 with Athena gives batch analysis and does not invoke the function when significant metrics are reported.

why: The Amazon VPC CNI plugin gives pods real VPC IP addresses. Its custom networking feature, configured with ENIConfig resources, places pod interfaces in specified subnets. Pods then talk natively and privately within the VPC and can use security groups for pods.

others.A: Transit Gateway connects VPCs and networks. It does not control which subnets EKS pods get IPs from.
others.B: Direct Connect is about on-premises connectivity and does not set pod subnets.
others.D: Network policies and anti-affinity rules control traffic and scheduling. They do not assign pods to custom subnets.

why: Changing an existing RDS instance to Multi-AZ is a single setting. RDS creates a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover and no data migration. That removes the single point of failure with the least effort.

others.B: Moving from relational MySQL to DynamoDB is a heterogeneous migration and requires a major rewrite.
others.C: Building a new instance and restoring from a snapshot takes manual work and loses data written since the snapshot.
others.D: RDS cannot run in an EC2 Auto Scaling group, and simple routing across separate databases would not keep the data consistent.

why: FSx for NetApp ONTAP is a managed file system that supports NFS and SMB on the same volumes, and multiprotocol access lets the same data be shared between Windows and Linux clients. A Multi-AZ deployment gives redundancy across Availability Zones.

others.B: Self-managed EC2 file servers are not managed, cannot share data between protocols, and lack AZ redundancy.
others.C: Two separate file systems cannot share the same data across both protocols, and FSx for Lustre is a high-performance computing file system, not a general NFS share.
others.D: S3 File Gateway runs as an appliance and fits hybrid caching. It is not a consolidated managed multi-protocol NAS in AWS.

tip: If you need NFS and SMB on the same data, choose FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

why: An Auto Scaling group of private instances across multiple AZs behind an ALB makes the web tier scalable and highly available. Aurora MySQL with a reader in another AZ gives automatic failover and offloads reads, which reduces read latency.

others.A: A single standby instance in another Region with failover routing does not scale and leaves the database unchanged.
others.D: An Auto Scaling group and an ALB are regional, so neither can span multiple Regions.
others.E: Cross-Region replicas add replication lag and do not reduce read latency for users in the primary Region.

why: Secrets Manager stores sensitive values encrypted with KMS and rotates them automatically on a schedule using rotation functions. A shared Lambda layer, such as the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension or a common retrieval library, lets thousands of functions fetch and cache the secrets the same way, with little ongoing overhead.

others.A: Lambda@Edge runs at CloudFront edge locations to change HTTP requests and responses. It is not a secrets store.
others.D: Parameter Store SecureString parameters have no built-in automatic rotation.
others.E: Dedicated-throughput consumers belong to Kinesis, and writing secrets into environment variables would break automatic rotation.

tip: If the question requires automatic secret rotation, choose Secrets Manager over Parameter Store.

why: Compute Optimizer gives rightsizing and cost recommendations for EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, and EBS volumes, as well as Lambda, ECS on Fargate, and more, all from one service. Turning it on covers every resource in the question with the least operational effort.

others.A: The Cost and Usage Report is raw billing data and contains no optimization recommendations.
others.B: Billing alerts warn about spend thresholds and do not give recommendations.
others.D: Compute Optimizer already covers Auto Scaling groups and EBS, so adding a CUR search is extra work for nothing.

why: Amazon EFS is a shared NFS file system that instances in every AZ of the VPC can mount at the same time through mount targets in the VPC. It gives high-performance shared access, and the traffic stays inside the VPC.

others.A: Calling the S3 APIs is object storage, not a shared file system, and by default the traffic goes to a public endpoint.
others.B: Mounting S3 as a volume needs third-party or Mountpoint tools and does not give full file system semantics or high performance.
others.C: An EBS volume lives in one AZ, and Multi-Attach works only for io1 and io2 within that AZ, so it cannot be shared across AZs.

tip: For a file system shared by instances in many AZs, choose EFS. EBS is limited to one AZ.

why: After the peak, the read replica runs at only 25% CPU, so it is oversized, while the primary at a steady 60% has reasonable headroom. Downsizing the replica cuts cost, keeps reporting reads off the primary, and leaves the primary sized for growth.

others.A: Deleting the replica would push the reporting load back onto the primary and raise its CPU.
others.C: Enlarging the underused replica and shrinking a primary at 60% CPU is the opposite of rightsizing.
others.D: Deleting the replica and enlarging the primary costs more and gives up the separation of read traffic.

why: For long-running, steady workloads, the largest discounts come from a 3-year term paid All Upfront. RDS Reserved Instances cover the PostgreSQL databases and an EC2 Instance Savings Plan covers the EC2 instances.

others.A: On-Demand RDS gets no discount, and a 1-year No Upfront Compute Savings Plan gives the smallest savings.
others.B: A 1-year No Upfront commitment gives lower discounts than a 3-year All Upfront one.
others.C: A 1-year Partial Upfront commitment is still less cost-effective than 3-year All Upfront.

tip: The deepest discount is the longest term with the most paid upfront.

why: IRSA works in two parts. You create an IAM role whose trust policy trusts the cluster's IAM OIDC identity provider, scoped to the service account's namespace and name. You then annotate the Kubernetes service account with the role ARN. Pods using that service account get temporary credentials for only that role.

others.A: Attaching policies to the node role gives the permissions to every pod on the node, which is not granular.
others.B: Kubernetes network policies control pod network traffic, not IAM permissions to AWS APIs.
others.C: The cluster IAM role is for the EKS control plane and is not passed to service accounts.

tip: IRSA means an OIDC provider, a role trust policy, and a service account annotation. EKS Pod Identity is the newer alternative.

why: SSE-KMS with the AWS managed key aws/s3 is rotated automatically every year. Its use is recorded in CloudTrail, and it has no monthly key charge, unlike a customer managed key, which costs 1 USD per month. Enabling S3 Bucket Keys cuts KMS request costs further.

others.A: With SSE-C the customer supplies and rotates the keys, so there is no automatic rotation or KMS tracking.
others.B: SSE-S3 keys are fully managed by S3 and are invisible to KMS and CloudTrail, so rotation cannot be tracked.
others.D: Customer managed keys support yearly rotation but cost 1 USD per key per month, so they do not minimize key cost.

why: Tagging resources by application and activating those tags as cost allocation tags in the Billing console lets Cost Explorer group and filter costs by application. Cost Explorer can also send regular reports. This is low cost and needs no extra infrastructure.

others.A: AWS Budgets tracks spend against thresholds and is not a per-application breakdown from untagged data.
others.B: Loading the CUR into RDS means paying for and running a database.
others.D: Tags must be activated as cost allocation tags before they appear in billing data, and downloading bills is manual.

tip: Tags only show up in cost reports after you activate them as cost allocation tags.

why: A multi-AZ Auto Scaling group keeps the web tier running if an AZ fails, and Multi-AZ RDS adds automatic database failover. CloudFront serves static assets from S3 with caching and durability. Together these give a resilient design for continuous service.

others.A: Putting everything in a single AZ is a single point of failure.
others.C: Single-AZ EC2 instances serving the static assets are still a single point of failure.
others.D: EFS One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, which undermines resilience, and it is a poor choice for web static assets.

why: A Gateway Load Balancer is built to put third-party security appliances inline. It forwards traffic transparently over GENEVE and scales the appliance fleet. Gateway Load Balancer endpoints in the application accounts' VPCs, which work through PrivateLink, steer traffic across accounts to the central appliances for inspection.

others.A: An NLB behind an interface endpoint is for exposing a service. It does not route traffic transparently inline for inspection.
others.B: An ALB is a layer 7 proxy that ends connections and cannot steer traffic to appliances in another account.
others.D: An interface endpoint cannot send traffic straight to an appliance. It needs a PrivateLink service, such as GWLB, behind it.

tip: Inline inspection with third-party firewall or IDS appliances means Gateway Load Balancer and GWLB endpoints.

why: An Aurora custom endpoint groups chosen DB instances, here the three replicas with different specs, and load balances connections across only those instances. The department's reporting queries are spread across them automatically.

others.B: A clone is a separate cluster that does not receive near-real-time production changes once it is created.
others.C: Instance endpoints point at one instance each, so the application would have to balance the load itself.
others.D: The reader endpoint balances across all six replicas, not just the three chosen ones.

tip: To send a workload to a subset of Aurora instances, use a custom endpoint.

why: Secrets Manager stores the RDS credentials encrypted and has built-in rotation for RDS for PostgreSQL, set here to every 30 days. Lambda fetches the secret at runtime. This is secure, managed credential handling with the least operational overhead.

others.A: Parameter Store has no built-in automatic rotation.
others.C: Writing your own rotation function and storing credentials in environment variables means more custom code and upkeep.
others.D: KMS stores encryption keys, not database credentials, and rotating the key does not change the password.

why: DMS Serverless provisions replication capacity automatically and scales it with the actual workload, measured in DMS capacity units, so it allocates only what is needed. It supports full load plus ongoing change data capture from Oracle to RDS for Oracle.

others.A: Multi-AZ adds high availability but does not right-size capacity for a load that varies through the day.
others.C: EC2 Auto Scaling cannot manage DMS replication instances.
others.D: DMS does not run on ECS or Fargate.

why: SaaS providers on AWS can publish an endpoint service behind an NLB. The consumer creates an interface VPC endpoint to it through AWS PrivateLink, and traffic then stays on the AWS network with private IPs and no internet exposure.

others.A: A Site-to-Site VPN connects to customer networks. It is not how you reach a SaaS service hosted on AWS, and it is heavier to run.
others.B: Transit Gateway needs the provider's VPC attached and exposes whole networks, not just one service.
others.C: PrivateLink is consumer-initiated and does not let the provider open connections into your VPC anyway. The real need is private access to the SaaS service, not an outbound-only setup.

tip: For private access to a SaaS service on AWS, use PrivateLink.

why: Site-to-Site VPN encrypts all traffic between the corporate network and the VPC with IPsec at the network layer. Route tables, security groups, and network ACLs then allow only the traffic that is needed, which prevents unrestricted access between the environments.

others.A: Direct Connect is not encrypted by default, and route tables are not fine-grained security controls.
others.B: IAM console restrictions do not provide network connectivity or encryption.
others.D: Transit Gateway alone does not encrypt traffic or connect to on premises. It would still need a VPN or Direct Connect attachment.

why: Secrets Manager removes the embedded credentials. The application loads them through an API call, which is a small code change. A rotation schedule, run by a Lambda rotation function that Secrets Manager provides for RDS MySQL, changes the password automatically.

others.A: KMS manages encryption keys, not database credentials, and rotating a key does not rotate the database password.
others.B: Encrypted local storage with a cron job is a custom, fragile solution that keeps secrets on the host.
others.D: Parameter Store cannot rotate credentials, and RDS has no rotation setting driven by Parameter Store.

why: Turning on CRR for the existing bucket, with S3 Batch Replication for objects already in it, replicates the data to the other Region. SSE-S3 provides encryption at rest at no extra cost or key management. Athena is serverless SQL directly on S3, so this has the least overhead.

others.A: Creating a new bucket and loading the data into it is extra work, and multi-Region KMS keys add management that the requirements do not need.
others.B: RDS is not serverless SQL over S3, and a new bucket means unnecessary data movement.
others.D: RDS cannot query data in S3 directly and is not serverless.

tip: For serverless SQL on data in S3, use Athena.

why: The uploaded images are used for training only twice a year, so Glacier Deep Archive's very low storage price fits, and its retrieval time of up to 48 hours is acceptable. Premium users need downloads at any time, which suits S3 Standard. Non-premium users download at most every 6 hours, which suits the cheaper Standard-IA with millisecond access.

others.B: Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours to retrieve, which is too slow for premium on-demand downloads.
others.C: One Zone-IA costs more than Deep Archive for data read only twice a year, and it lacks multi-AZ resilience.
others.D: Glacier Flexible Retrieval is too slow for user downloads, and One Zone-IA costs more for the training images.

why: An SQS queue buffers the asynchronous batch requests. ECS services poll it and scale task count and cluster capacity, through capacity providers, based on queue depth, scaling to zero for models that sit idle. Containers can load 1 GB of model data into memory once and reuse it.

others.A: An NLB cannot invoke Lambda, since only ALB supports Lambda targets, and loading 1 GB per cold start is inefficient.
others.B: An ALB is for synchronous requests. For asynchronous bursts, scaling on queue depth handles load better.
others.C: You cannot auto scale the vCPUs of a Lambda function. They are set by its memory setting.

why: A 30-minute RTO with no active use of the DR site fits pilot light or warm standby. A minimal Auto Scaling group and ALB in a second Region, an Aurora global database with replication lag usually under 1 second and managed failover, and Route 53 active-passive failover meet the RTO at low cost.

others.B: An Auto Scaling group cannot span Regions, and active-active is not needed while the primary is healthy.
others.C: Restoring Aurora from a backup can exceed 30 minutes, and active-active is unnecessary.
others.D: AWS Backup cannot back up and recreate whole infrastructure configurations such as ALBs and Auto Scaling groups.

why: The batch jobs cannot be disrupted, so they need On-Demand capacity rather than Spot. The data is read for 30 days in S3 Standard. It is then kept only for retention, so Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest place for it, and an expiration rule deletes it at 2 years.

others.A: Spot Instances can interrupt the jobs, and Glacier Instant Retrieval costs more than Deep Archive for data that is only retained.
others.B: Glacier Instant Retrieval for the first 30 days of active access has high retrieval fees and a 90-day minimum storage charge.
others.C: Spot Instances can interrupt the jobs, which cannot be disrupted.

why: Direct Connect gives private, consistent low-latency links that meet the single-digit latency need. A transit VIF to a Direct Connect gateway, with that gateway associated with the existing transit gateway, reaches all attached VPCs over one connection, which is cost-effective.

others.A: VPN connections to each VPC run over the internet with variable latency and add many tunnels to manage.
others.C: Site-to-Site VPN cannot attach to a Direct Connect gateway in that way. VPN latency is variable anyway.
others.E: VPN connections to the transit gateway go over the internet and cannot guarantee low, consistent latency.

why: RDS Proxy keeps a pool of connections to the database. During a Multi-AZ failover it reroutes to the new primary without waiting for DNS to propagate, cutting failover times by up to 66% and keeping client connections open. That reduces timeouts.

others.B: A read replica offloads reads but does not change how long a Multi-AZ failover takes.
others.C: Performance Insights only shows where load comes from and does not reduce failover time.
others.D: Cross-Region snapshots support disaster recovery but do not speed up failover.

tip: For faster RDS failover or connection storms, use RDS Proxy.

why: EventBridge Scheduler or scheduled rules run cron expressions for business hours and invoke Lambda functions. The functions call StartDBInstance and StopDBInstance on the instances that have the development tag. It is simple, serverless, and needs little upkeep.

others.A: CloudWatch alarms respond to metric thresholds, not to a time schedule.
others.B: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations and cannot drive a start and stop schedule.
others.C: State Manager can run Automation runbooks on a schedule, but the keyed answer treats an EventBridge schedule as the simpler pattern.

tip: Anything that runs on a time schedule points to EventBridge Scheduler or scheduled rules.

why: Requester Pays makes the requester's account, here the marketing firm, pay the request and data transfer charges for downloads from the bucket. The bucket owner's data transfer costs drop to nothing.

others.B: Cross-Region Replication makes the company pay for inter-Region transfer and for replicating years of data.
others.C: S3 buckets cannot be shared through AWS Resource Access Manager in this way, and it would not change who pays for transfer.
others.D: Intelligent-Tiering optimizes storage class, and syncing to another bucket still incurs transfer charges.

why: AWS WAF can be associated with the ALB. A rate-based rule automatically blocks IP addresses that go over a request threshold, which mitigates HTTP flood DDoS attacks at layer 7. Global Accelerator already brings Shield Standard protection at layers 3 and 4, so adding WAF to the ALB takes the least effort.

others.A: AWS WAF cannot be associated with a Global Accelerator accelerator.
others.B: A custom Lambda function that updates network ACLs takes a lot of effort, and network ACLs have low rule limits.
others.D: CloudFront cannot use a Global Accelerator accelerator as its origin in this design, and the change would re-architect the entry point.

why: The AWS Glue DynamoDB export connector uses DynamoDB's export to S3 feature, which relies on point-in-time recovery. The export reads from backups and does not use the table's provisioned read capacity, so the daily metric jobs have minimal effect on the live table.

others.A: The Athena DynamoDB connector scans the live table and uses its read capacity.
others.C: A Redshift COPY from DynamoDB reads the table directly and uses provisioned read capacity.
others.D: EMR Hive external tables over DynamoDB scan the table and use read capacity.

tip: If an analytics job must not consume a DynamoDB table's capacity, export the table to S3 first.

why: An SQS queue stores jobs durably and decouples the producers from the workers. Scaling the Auto Scaling group on the number of messages in the queue, ideally the backlog per instance, adds and removes instances to match the job count, and the instances process jobs in parallel.

others.A: SNS pushes messages to subscribers and does not store jobs durably, and CPU usage does not reflect the job backlog.
others.B: Network usage does not reflect how many jobs are waiting.
others.D: SNS does not store jobs, and the number of published messages does not show how much work is outstanding.

tip: For durable jobs plus worker scaling, use SQS and scale on queue depth.

why: ECS on Fargate runs modular containerized services with no servers to manage. RDS Multi-AZ keeps the structured relational schemas with managed high availability, and S3 is the scalable, low-cost place to store product images. This has the least operational overhead.

others.A: Containers on self-managed EC2 instances add overhead, and storing images in RDS is inefficient.
others.B: DynamoDB does not keep the structured relational schemas, and lifting a monolith into Lambda is impractical.
others.C: EKS on EC2 adds operational overhead, and Glacier Deep Archive is far too slow for serving product images.

why: Encrypting the data before it is stored in S3 means encrypting on the client side, before upload. Client-side encryption with customer managed keys, for example through the AWS Encryption SDK with a KMS key, makes sure S3 receives only ciphertext.

others.B: With SSE-KMS, S3 encrypts the data after it arrives, so the data is not encrypted before it reaches S3.
others.C: SSE-C is still server-side encryption: S3 encrypts with your key after receiving plaintext over HTTPS.
others.D: S3 managed keys are used only for server-side encryption and cannot be used for client-side encryption.

tip: The phrase before storing in S3 or before sending means client-side encryption.

why: EMR runtime roles let each team's job, submitted as an EMR step or through Lake Formation, assume its own IAM role with only the permissions that team needs. When runtime roles are enabled, EMR blocks workloads from using the instance profile through IMDS, which meets the requirement to deny IMDSv2 access.

others.A: VPC endpoints give private network paths but do not limit each team's IAM permissions or block IMDS.
others.C: An instance profile is shared across the whole cluster and is reached through IMDS, which is exactly what must be avoided.
others.D: Setting the application-scoped IAM role option to false does not give each team scoped roles.

why: An SQS FIFO queue provides exactly-once processing through deduplication IDs within a 5-minute window, preserves ordering, and stores messages durably across multiple AZs. That decouples the web and worker tiers without losing data or processing a form twice.

others.B: API Gateway forwards requests but does not durably store and forward messages to workers.
others.C: A standard queue delivers at least once, so a form can be processed more than once.
others.D: A synchronous Step Functions workflow tightly couples the tiers and is not a buffer between them.

tip: The phrase exactly once means an SQS FIFO queue.

why: Kinesis Data Streams ingests streaming data from many producers in real time, with Firehose or a consumer loading it continuously into OpenSearch Service. OpenSearch gives near-real-time full-text search and analytics, and QuickSight builds visualizations.

others.A: Self-managed EC2 ingestion plus Athena queries over S3 is not real-time search.
others.B: EMR and Redshift Spectrum are batch analytics, not real-time search.
others.C: DynamoDB with CloudWatch dashboards does not give full-text search.

why: AWS App2Container analyzes existing .NET or Java applications and containerizes them, producing CloudFormation templates for ECS or EKS. Deploying to ECS on Fargate removes server management, and ECS Service Auto Scaling uses CloudWatch metrics, so this has the least operational overhead.

others.B: ECS on EC2 instances means managing and patching the container hosts.
others.C: App Runner does not containerize applications and does not deploy to ECS. It runs services from code or images on its own platform.
others.D: App Runner does not containerize applications or deploy to EKS, and EKS on EC2 adds overhead.

why: Secrets Manager is the managed service for storing credentials securely, and its BatchGetSecretValue API retrieves several secrets in one call. Using it directly, with CloudFormation to provision the secrets, has the least overhead.

others.A: BatchGetSecretValue is a Secrets Manager API, not a Parameter Store API.
others.B: AWS Batch is a compute job scheduler and is not needed to call a Secrets Manager API.
others.C: Parameter Store does not offer BatchGetSecretValue, and AWS Batch is unnecessary.

why: A CloudFront distribution in front of the S3 bucket caches the 100 software files at edge locations around the world. Once the files are cached, thousands of remote servers download from a nearby edge instead of from Tokyo, which cuts deployment latency with little to manage. Signed URLs keep access restricted.

others.A: CloudFront is global, not regional, and turning caching off removes the latency benefit.
others.B: Adding a second bucket in us-east-1 with origin failover improves availability, not latency, and adds replication to manage.
others.C: Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance transfers but does not cache, so every server still pulls each file from the origin.

tip: Many clients downloading the same files means a caching CDN, so choose CloudFront.

why: FSx for NetApp ONTAP Multi-AZ provides block storage over iSCSI, with synchronous replication and automatic failover across AZs. An active-standby pair of EC2 instances can both reach the same LUN, giving low-latency, highly available block storage without custom replication.

others.A: FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB file storage, not block storage.
others.B: Replicating EBS volumes at the application level takes considerable implementation effort.
others.D: EBS has no native replication across AZs, because volumes are tied to one AZ.

tip: For shared block storage across AZs, use FSx for NetApp ONTAP over iSCSI.

why: The ALB's security group needs three rules. An inbound rule allows HTTPS on port 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 for public clients. An outbound rule allows port 443 to the web instances for forwarded traffic. Another outbound rule allows port 8443 to the instances for health checks. Security groups are stateful, so response traffic does not need its own rules.

others.B: Allowing all outbound traffic to 0.0.0.0/0 is broader than needed, so least privilege points to the instance targets.
others.D: Inbound rules from the instances are not needed, because responses are allowed automatically by stateful tracking.
others.F: The ALB starts the health checks, so they need an outbound rule, not an inbound one.

tip: Security groups are stateful: allow the direction in which the connection is opened.

why: CloudFront accepts custom-domain certificates only from ACM in us-east-1. Origin access control signs CloudFront's requests to S3 with SigV4 and supports PUT and POST uploads, so the bucket policy can allow uploads only from the distribution through OAC.

others.B: CloudFront cannot use ACM certificates from eu-west-1.
others.C: Transfer Acceleration is a separate S3 feature and not how uploads through CloudFront are authorized.
others.E: S3 website endpoints do not support uploads or OAC, and they serve only GET requests over HTTP.

tip: Certificates for CloudFront must come from ACM in us-east-1.

why: Athena runs SQL directly on Parquet files in S3, supports reading CSE-KMS encrypted data when the table is configured for it, and charges only per TB scanned. The daily prefixes allow partition pruning, which makes it the cheapest choice for occasional queries.

others.B: S3 Select does not support client-side encrypted objects or moving-average queries, and it is closed to new customers.
others.C: Redshift Spectrum needs a Redshift cluster or Serverless workgroup, which costs more for occasional queries.
others.D: EMR Serverless with Spark SQL takes more setup and costs more than Athena for occasional sampling.

tip: For occasional SQL on S3, choose Athena.

why: Geoproximity routing sends users to the resource that is geographically closest to them, and you can shift that with a bias. That matches the requirement to reach the closest EC2 instances. Within each Region, an internet-facing NLB spreads traffic across the AZs.

others.A: Geolocation routing chooses a target by the user's country or continent, not the nearest Region, so users near a border can be sent farther away.
others.C: Multivalue answer routing returns random healthy records and ignores location.
others.D: Weighted routing splits traffic by fixed ratios, not by the user's location.

tip: Geolocation follows where the user is, for example by country. Geoproximity follows physical distance and can be biased.

why: RDS encryption at rest with KMS is a single setting at creation time and covers storage, backups, snapshots, and replicas. For encryption in transit, TLS is used: RDS supplies server certificates, and ACM can provide TLS certificates for the application endpoints such as an ALB. Both are managed, so this has the least operational overhead.

others.B: Running IPsec tunnels between EC2 and RDS inside a VPC adds operational complexity that is not needed.
others.C: Third-party application-level encryption adds code and key management overhead.
others.D: A VPN is meant for connecting outside networks and is not needed to encrypt traffic between EC2 and RDS.

why: An AWS Backup plan can keep RDS snapshots for 90 days and can also turn on continuous backups, which give point-in-time restore for up to 35 days and so cover the 14-day need, all under one managed policy. RDS automated backups alone are capped at 35 days of retention.

others.A: RDS automated backup retention has a maximum of 35 days, so it cannot be set to 90 days.
others.B: Taking and deleting daily manual snapshots is operational work and does not give point-in-time restore.
others.C: Aurora cloning does not exist for RDS for Oracle, and a clone is not a backup.

tip: RDS automated backups top out at 35 days. For longer retention, use AWS Backup or manual snapshots.

why: Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity, measured in ACUs, up and down in fine increments with actual load, so a variable, read-heavy relational workload pays only for what it uses. It is fully managed and can add readers as growth continues.

others.A: Provisioned IOPS storage is billed whether or not it is used, which is costly for variable demand.
others.C: DynamoDB is not relational, and the application needs a relational database.
others.D: Magnetic storage is previous generation with poor performance and is not recommended.

why: A gateway endpoint sends S3 traffic privately at no charge. A Deny statement in the instance profile policy with the condition s3:ResourceAccount (or aws:ResourceAccount) not equal to the company's account ID blocks access to any bucket outside the account. That covers every customer bucket, including new ones, without listing each bucket.

others.A: Listing specific buckets in the policy has to be updated every time a customer bucket is added, which is more overhead.
others.B: A NAT gateway costs money, security groups cannot filter by AWS service, and nothing limits access to the company's own buckets.
others.D: A NAT gateway adds cost, and keeping deny statements in every bucket policy is more work than one identity policy.

tip: To limit access to your own account's buckets, use a Deny with the aws:ResourceAccount or s3:ResourceAccount condition.

why: The company already uses IAM Identity Center. Permission sets give granular, least-privilege access to RDS and S3, and assigning them to team groups provisions short-term role credentials in each account. This is central and needs the least management.

others.A: Hand-building IAM roles for each team in each account takes more effort than using permission sets.
others.C: Individual IAM users mean long-term credentials and higher management overhead.
others.D: Creating a separate account for each team with cross-account roles adds a lot of overhead.

why: IAM Roles Anywhere lets workloads outside AWS, such as these on-premises virtual machines, use X.509 certificates from a trusted certificate authority to get temporary credentials for an IAM role. The VMs can then reach the S3 bucket without long-lived access keys.

others.A: Allowing access by IP address alone does not authenticate the application.
others.C: IAM user access keys on the VM are long-lived credentials, which goes against the requirement for temporary access.
others.D: Keeping IAM user keys in Secrets Manager still relies on long-lived credentials.

tip: For workloads outside AWS that need temporary credentials, use IAM Roles Anywhere.

why: A transit gateway, shared to the new accounts with AWS Resource Access Manager, connects all VPCs to one Direct Connect gateway through a transit VIF. Every account gets consistent, low-latency access to the on-premises directory and DNS services over the existing Direct Connect link.

others.A: A separate Direct Connect connection for each account is expensive and slow to provision.
others.B: VPC endpoints reach AWS services or PrivateLink services. They do not route traffic to on-premises servers.
others.C: A VPN connection for each account adds tunnels to manage and gives less consistent performance.

why: CloudFront in front of the existing ALB speeds up dynamic content over the AWS global network, using persistent connections and TCP optimizations at edge locations, and caches whatever can be cached. It serves millions of users worldwide without running compute in more Regions, which keeps cost down.

others.B: Route 53 geolocation routing with only one Region does not bring content closer to users.
others.C: S3 website hosting serves only static content, not a dynamic application.
others.D: Direct Connect is a private link to on-premises networks and does not deliver content to the public.

why: S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves each object between access tiers automatically based on how it is used, so data left untouched for months becomes cheaper, with no retrieval fees and no performance impact. It keeps 11 nines of durability and stores data across multiple AZs.

others.A: S3 Standard charges the full rate for data that sits unused for months.
others.C: Deep Archive retrieval takes hours, which does not suit data in continuous use.
others.D: One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, which lowers availability and resilience.

tip: Unknown or changing access patterns point to S3 Intelligent-Tiering.

why: Amazon EFS is an NFS file system that many instances in an Auto Scaling group can mount at once across AZs. It is regional, highly available, and elastic, and applications use it like a POSIX file system with minimal code changes. General Purpose performance mode suits typical workloads.

others.A: A single NFS server on EC2 is a single point of failure.
others.B: Single-AZ FSx for Windows File Server uses SMB, which is not native to Linux, and it is not highly available.
others.C: EBS volumes attach to one instance in one AZ and cannot be shared by an Auto Scaling group.

why: A Network Load Balancer handles TCP traffic at layer 4 with high performance across AZs. An Auto Scaling group adds and removes instances automatically as the number of users changes. Together they provide high availability and scale automatically at low cost.

others.C: An ALB handles only HTTP and HTTPS and does not suit raw TCP clients.
others.D: Adding instances by hand is not automatic scaling.
others.E: A Gateway Load Balancer is for inline security appliances, not for application traffic.

why: An Organizations tag policy sets the allowed values, sensitive and nonsensitive, for the tag key and can enforce them for EC2 instances. SCPs block actions: one denies ec2:RunInstances when aws:RequestTag for the key is missing (a Null condition), and another denies ec2:DeleteTags.

others.B: An SCP cannot define allowed tag values in the way a tag policy does.
others.C: Tag policies cannot deny instance launches or tag deletions. They only standardize tag keys and values.
others.E: Detecting problems and deleting resources afterward is reactive, and it can delete resources by mistake.

tip: Tag policies standardize keys and values. SCPs deny actions such as launching untagged instances or deleting tags.

why: Setting the automated backup retention period to 30 days keeps automated backups for the required time and removes older ones at no extra cost. Manual snapshots never expire on their own, so those older than 30 days must be deleted, which here is done manually. Existing backups younger than 30 days are kept.

others.A: Bringing in AWS Backup is not necessary, because RDS retention can be set directly.
others.B: Disabling automated backups deletes the existing automated backups, which the company wants to keep.
others.D: Disabling automated backups removes the existing ones, and CloudFormation is not a tool for deleting snapshots.

why: Amazon EFS is a fully managed, elastic file system that uses NFS v4.0 and v4.1. The legacy application can keep using NFS with no changes.

others.A: DataSync is a data transfer service, not storage.
others.B: EBS is block storage attached to one instance and does not speak NFS.
others.D: EMRFS lets EMR clusters use S3 and is not an NFS share.

why: An SQS queue durably buffers incoming tracker data, keeping messages for up to 14 days, so bursts no longer overwhelm the EC2 application. The instances poll and process at their own pace, and messages stay in the queue until they are deleted after processing, so no data is lost. It is fully managed.

others.A: Scanning an S3 bucket for new objects is inefficient and needs custom tracking of what has been processed.
others.B: Lambda behind API Gateway could hit concurrency throttling and gives no buffer for replay, and the processing would have to be rewritten.
others.D: Polling a DynamoDB table needs custom logic to track processed items and adds overhead.

tip: If an application is overwhelmed or losing data, decouple it with an SQS queue.

why: Keeping the RDS cluster in private subnets means it has no public exposure. A Site-to-Site VPN from the office customer gateway encrypts traffic and gives the desktop client private connectivity only from the office network, which makes it the most secure option.

others.A: Public subnets expose the database without need, even with a VPN in place.
others.C: Private subnets cannot be reached from the office over the internet without a VPN or Direct Connect, so allowing office IPs in a security group is not enough.
others.D: Public subnets with only security groups and database users expose the cluster to the internet.

why: Data moving between EC2 instances in the same AZ over private IPs costs nothing, while traffic between AZs is charged at about 0.01 USD per GB in each direction. Putting all the batch-processing instances in one AZ removes the inter-instance transfer charges. Transfer between S3 and EC2 in the same Region is also free.

others.A: An Auto Scaling group does not decide where instances are placed in a way that reduces transfer charges.
others.B: Keeping everything in one Region still incurs inter-AZ charges if instances are spread across AZs.
others.D: Spreading instances across multiple AZs is what incurs inter-AZ data transfer charges.

tip: For lowest cost on heavy east-west traffic, keep the instances in one AZ, accepting the trade-off in availability.

why: Secrets Manager encrypts the secret with a KMS key and integrates natively with Aurora. Its managed rotation can be set to a custom schedule of every 14 days, with no custom rotation code, so it takes the least effort.

others.B: Parameter Store cannot rotate secrets, so you would have to write and maintain a custom Lambda function.
others.C: Keeping credentials in a file on EFS with a custom rotation function is fragile and requires significant operational effort.
others.D: Keeping credentials in a file in S3 with custom rotation is insecure and requires significant operational effort.

why: Processing terabyte-sized videos for up to 20 minutes goes beyond Lambda's 15-minute limit and storage limits. ECS on Fargate scales containers with demand and has no servers to manage. Aurora stores the metadata, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering keeps storage costs down for video whose access patterns vary.

others.A: Lambda's 15-minute timeout and limited ephemeral storage cannot handle 20-minute jobs on terabyte-sized videos.
others.C: An ALB in front of batch processing workers is unnecessary, and running EC2 fleets adds management work.
others.D: Glacier Deep Archive is too slow to retrieve for videos that users watch daily, and single-AZ RDS is not resilient.

why: With AWS Fargate for EKS, each pod runs on serverless compute that AWS provisions and manages. Fargate profiles choose which pods run on Fargate. There are no nodes to patch or scale, so this has the least operational overhead.

others.A: Self-managed nodes leave the company managing the EC2 compute.
others.B: Managed node groups still run EC2 instances in your account that you have to look after, such as handling AMI updates.
others.D: Karpenter improves node provisioning but still leaves the company managing EC2 nodes and the Karpenter configuration.

tip: If the question says not to manage compute for EKS or ECS, choose Fargate.

why: Aurora Serverless v2 is a managed relational database that scales capacity automatically with application traffic and is billed for the capacity used. It includes continuous automated backups stored in S3. This meets the needs for structured data, scaling, and backups cost-effectively.

others.A: A self-managed database on Spot Instances risks interruption and data loss and adds operational burden.
others.B: RDS has no on-demand capacity mode, and a provisioned instance does not scale automatically with traffic.
others.D: A NoSQL database does not fit structured transactional data, and running it yourself on EC2 adds overhead.

why: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 adds a route, using the S3 prefix list, to the subnet's route table. S3 traffic from the instance then stays on the AWS private network instead of going over the public internet. Gateway endpoints for S3 cost nothing.

others.B: An S3 bucket cannot be moved into a VPC.
others.C: Access points control access permissions but still use public S3 endpoints unless they are combined with a VPC endpoint.
others.D: Direct Connect connects on-premises networks to AWS. It is not a path from a VPC to S3.

why: The product catalog is read-heavy and rarely updated, which makes it ideal for caching. ElastiCache for Redis with lazy loading serves repeated searches from memory, which cuts CPU on the database and makes searches much faster.

others.A: Redshift is an analytics data warehouse and is not suited to low-latency, transactional website lookups.
others.C: Adding web servers increases the load on the overloaded database.
others.D: The Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads, and throttling queries makes the user experience worse.

tip: For data that is read often and changes rarely, cache it in ElastiCache.

why: The on-premises storage is block storage and is running out of space. Volume Gateway cached volumes present iSCSI block volumes, keep the full data set in S3, and cache frequently used data locally for low-latency access. That expands capacity into the cloud with little management.

others.A: S3 File Gateway provides file shares over SMB or NFS, not block storage, so applications would need to change.
others.C: Stored volumes keep the full data set on premises, which does not solve the shortage of local capacity.
others.D: Tape Gateway is for backup and archive, not low-latency application data.

tip: Cached volumes keep primary data in S3 with a local cache. Stored volumes keep primary data on premises with asynchronous backup to S3.

why: SQS queues decouple collection from fulfillment and hold orders durably, so nothing is lost when instances scale in or out. Scaling each Auto Scaling group on its queue depth, ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible or the backlog per instance, sizes each tier to its own workload.

others.A: Setting minimum capacity to peak wastes money, and CPU usage does not reflect backlog.
others.B: Creating new Auto Scaling groups through SNS is an anti-pattern, and there is still no durable buffer for orders.
others.C: SQS does not send scaling notifications. Scaling is based on CloudWatch queue metrics.

why: DynamoDB global tables replicate active-active across Regions automatically, which gives continuous availability and resilience to a Region failure. Provisioned capacity with auto scaling is usually cheaper than on-demand for a steady, growing user base.

others.A: This option is contradictory, because global tables require replica tables in multiple Regions, and on-demand costs more for steady traffic.
others.B: DynamoDB has no manual Cross-Region Replication feature. Global tables replace it, and DAX adds cost without adding resilience.
others.C: Building your own replication with Streams duplicates what global tables already do and adds overhead.

why: S3 File Gateway runs on premises as a VM or appliance. It presents the S3 data over NFS or SMB with a local cache, so the rendering application gets low-latency access while the data stays in low-cost S3.

others.A: Mountpoint for S3 has no local caching gateway, so latency to S3 over the WAN would hurt rendering performance.
others.C: Copying data to FSx for Windows File Server adds storage cost and duplicates the data.
others.D: Building a custom file server on the S3 API means more development and upkeep.

why: Global Accelerator sends international users into the AWS global network at the nearest edge location using anycast static IPs, avoiding congested internet paths to us-east-1. This lowers API latency for dynamic, uncacheable traffic without moving the ERP system.

others.A: Direct Connect for each customer data center is very expensive and slow to set up.
others.B: The CachingOptimized policy caches responses, which is inappropriate for dynamic API exchanges and could return stale or wrong data.
others.D: VPN tunnels to every customer network add overhead and still run over the internet.

tip: For non-cacheable or TCP traffic from global users to a single Region, choose Global Accelerator.

why: API Gateway feeding SQS absorbs bursts of thousands of survey responses an hour. Lambda processes them, Amazon Comprehend performs natural language sentiment analysis, and DynamoDB stores the results, with TTL deleting records after 365 days. Every part is serverless and scales automatically.

others.B: An API on a single EC2 instance does not scale and is a single point of failure.
others.C: Amazon Rekognition analyzes images and video, not the sentiment of text.
others.D: Amazon Lex builds chatbots and is not a sentiment analysis service, and SQS does not push to Lambda. Lambda polls the queue.

tip: Comprehend handles text and sentiment, Rekognition handles images and video, and Lex builds chatbots.

why: The AWSEC2-PatchLoadBalancerInstance Automation runbook deregisters an instance from its load balancer target group, patches it, and registers it again. Running it through Systems Manager Maintenance Windows removes instances from service on schedule during patching, which avoids the errors.

others.A: Changing the target type would mean recreating the target group, and it does not take instances out of service during patching.
others.B: The current document is causing the errors, so leaving it unchanged does not fix anything.
others.E: State Manager keeps instances in a desired configuration. It does not coordinate deregistering instances, and health checks react only after a failure.

why: The data must be encrypted where it is processed, before it reaches S3, with customer-specific keys. That points to client-side encryption with a separate KMS key for each customer. Serverless Glue jobs, one per customer with its own security configuration and KMS key, avoid managing clusters, so this takes the least operational effort.

others.A: SSE-S3 is server-side encryption with keys that S3 manages, so the keys are not customer-specific and the data is not encrypted before it is stored.
others.B: A separate EMR cluster for each customer with a custom client-side root key means a lot of cluster and key management.
others.D: SSE-KMS encrypts on the server side after the data arrives in S3, and EMR clusters for each customer add overhead.

tip: In practice, Glue security configurations offer SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS for S3 targets, while EMR supports CSE-KMS. For the exam, client-side encryption with KMS keys per customer is the intended idea.

why: The application is stateless and resilient, so it can tolerate Spot interruptions. An Auto Scaling group built from a launch template with the AMI, using Spot capacity, behind an ALB scales out and in automatically during busy periods at the lowest compute price.

others.A: A fixed second On-Demand instance does not scale seamlessly and costs more than Spot.
others.B: Weighted DNS routing across two fixed instances has no health-aware load balancing and does not scale automatically.
others.C: Stopping the instance to resize it causes downtime and is not seamless scaling.

tip: For stateless, interruption-tolerant workloads, an Auto Scaling group with Spot capacity is the most cost-effective option. In practice, use the group's mixed instances policy.

why: An S3 Bucket Key creates a short-lived bucket-level key from KMS and uses it to generate data keys for objects locally in S3. That cuts KMS requests and costs by up to 99% for objects accessed often, while keeping SSE-KMS encryption. It applies to new objects, or to existing ones once they are copied again.

others.A: SSE-S3 drops KMS altogether, which may break the strict encryption requirement to use KMS keys.
others.C: Client-side encryption still calls KMS for data keys and adds application complexity.
others.D: SSE-C keys are supplied with each request and are not stored or managed in KMS.

tip: If the goal is to reduce KMS request costs for SSE-KMS, turn on S3 Bucket Keys.

why: AWS Application Migration Service is the rehost, or lift-and-shift, tool. You install the Replication Agent on each VM for continuous block-level replication. After the initial sync, you launch test instances for acceptance testing, then stop the source operations and launch cutover instances to finish the migration quickly.

others.A: The Schema Conversion Tool converts database schemas and does not collect VM data or migrate servers.
others.E: App2Container containerizes applications, which is replatforming, not lift-and-shift.
others.F: DMS migrates databases, not whole VMs.

tip: Lift-and-shift of servers means AWS Application Migration Service: install the agent, replicate, test, then cut over.

why: A Cognito identity pool exchanges user pool tokens for temporary IAM credentials, scoped by policy for example to each user's own prefix, so users can access S3 securely. An S3 VPC endpoint lets the application in the private subnet reach S3 privately without going over the internet.

others.B: User pools issue JWTs for authentication. They cannot give out AWS credentials for S3 without an identity pool.
others.D: A NAT gateway sends traffic over the internet and adds cost, and S3 cannot tell whether a request came from Cognito.
others.E: Restricting the bucket to user IP addresses is unworkable for users on varying networks and does not authenticate them.

tip: User pools handle authentication and issue JWTs. Identity pools issue temporary AWS credentials.

why: The peaks are unpredictable, and the processing tier is overwhelmed while the queue fills up. A target tracking policy on SQS queue depth, ideally the backlog per instance, scales the processing instances out as messages pile up and back in when the queue drains, which reduces delays.

others.A: Scheduled scaling cannot handle peaks that are variable and unpredictable.
others.B: Caching DynamoDB does not fix CPU saturation on the processing tier.
others.C: CloudFront caching for the web tier does nothing for the overloaded queue workers.

why: The keyed answer matches capacity to usage. Scheduled Reserved Instances gave discounted, uninterruptible capacity for a recurring window such as 12 hours on Sunday, and Standard Reserved Instances give the deepest discount for instances that run constantly.

others.B: A Convertible Reserved Instance bills around the clock, so paying for it to cover only 12 hours a week is wasteful.
others.C: Spot Instances can be interrupted, and the Sunday workload cannot tolerate interruptions.
others.D: Spot Instances can be interrupted, and Convertible Reserved Instances give a smaller discount than Standard ones.

tip: AWS no longer sells Scheduled Reserved Instances. Today you would use On-Demand Instances, or On-Demand Capacity Reservations, for the Sunday window.

why: AWS Batch manages compute for image processing jobs and scales it automatically. It can run on Fargate or managed compute environments, so there is no infrastructure to manage. Step Functions orchestrates the workflow steps and removes manual tasks, and S3 stores the large output files cheaply and without limits.

others.A: ECS on EC2 Spot means managing instances, SQS is a queue rather than a workflow orchestrator, and EFS costs more than S3 for outputs.
others.C: EC2 Spot Instances bring infrastructure to manage, and there is no workflow orchestration.
others.D: Self-managed EC2 instances and a single EBS volume mean operational overhead and limited scalability.

why: CloudFront caches images at edge locations, which speeds up downloads for users around the world. S3 Transfer Acceleration sends uploads through edge locations over the AWS backbone to the bucket. Both are configuration changes that need little implementation effort.

others.B: Moving to EC2 instances in several Regions is a major re-architecture.
others.C: Multi-Region buckets with replication and redirect logic take much more work than needed.
others.D: S3 cannot be a standard Global Accelerator endpoint for this purpose, and the option ignores caching downloads.

tip: For downloads, use CloudFront. For uploads to S3 over long distances, use S3 Transfer Acceleration.

why: An S3 gateway endpoint adds a route to the route table so S3 API traffic from the private subnet stays on the AWS network and bypasses the NAT gateway and internet. Gateway endpoints for S3 have no hourly or data processing charges, so this is the most cost-effective option.

others.A: Interface endpoints also keep traffic private but cost money per hour and per GB.
others.C: Traffic through a NAT gateway still goes to the public S3 endpoint, and a bucket policy does not change the path.
others.D: A second NAT gateway still sends traffic toward the internet and adds cost.

tip: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB and are free, so prefer them for cost.

why: Separate Kubernetes service accounts linked to separate IAM roles through IRSA give each set of pods only its own permissions: S3 for the data services and DynamoDB for the UI. Pod credentials come from the service account's role, not from the node.

others.A: Putting both policies on the instance profile gives every pod access to both services, and Kubernetes RBAC cannot limit AWS API access.
others.B: IAM policies cannot be attached directly to pods.
others.D: This swaps the access, giving the UI S3 and the data services DynamoDB, which is the opposite of what is required.

tip: Full-access managed policies are broader than least privilege. A scoped custom policy is better in practice.

why: AD Connector proxies authentication to the existing on-premises Active Directory without copying the directory. Connecting it to IAM Identity Center lets AD groups be mapped to permission sets across all accounts in the organization, which gives central identity management with the least overhead.

others.A: Running AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a trust and roles for each account adds a directory to run and more manual setup.
others.B: Individual IAM users are not centralized and create heavy management overhead.
others.D: Cognito handles identities for customer-facing applications, not workforce access to AWS accounts.

tip: For workforce access across Organizations with an existing AD, use IAM Identity Center with AD Connector or a trust with AWS Managed Microsoft AD.

why: An API Gateway resource policy can allow or deny calls based on the source IP address, using aws:SourceIp, or on the VPC endpoint. A policy that denies any IP not on the trusted list makes the API reachable only from the company's internal network ranges.

others.A: Private integrations connect API Gateway to backends inside a VPC and do not filter client IP addresses.
others.C: API Gateway is a managed service and cannot be deployed into a private subnet with network ACLs.
others.D: API Gateway endpoints have no security groups for you to change.

tip: In practice, resource policies are supported only on REST APIs. For HTTP APIs, use a Lambda authorizer or WAF in front.
